title: All shall be well
hookLine: Julian is told that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well (Revelations of Divine Love 27)
last: A SIDE THE WORLD'S MEASURING STICK MISSES.

lines: SAID FAST, IT SOUNDS LIKE: IT'LL BE FINE.
JULIAN HEARD IT IN THE BED.
SHE WAS ASKING A HARD QUESTION.
cards: All shall be well. Said fast, it can sound like it'll be fine, something said over a shoulder on the way out of a room. But the woman who wrote it down heard it in her sickbed.

Julian of Norwich, whom this path met with a hazelnut in her palm, writes that she was so ill the people around her thought she was dying. And she wasn't asking for comfort. She was asking a hard question.

teach.h: WHY WASN'T SIN STOPPED AT THE START?
teach.b: First, the question. In chapter twenty-seven of her Revelations of Divine Love, Julian says she wondered why God, in all his foreseeing wisdom, didn't stop sin at the very beginning.
Then, she thought, all would have been well. It's the old why, asked straight, by someone in pain. Second, the answer.
She doesn't get a reason. She hears that sin was behovely, an old word for fitting, something that had its place.
And then the line, in Grace Warrack's edition: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Third, the tone.

In her telling, the words came very tenderly, with no blame laid on her, nor on any who shall be saved. Not a lecture, not a correction for asking. A promise, said kindly to a person who had dared the question.
Not all is well: all shall be. Julian doesn't pretend the world in front of her is fine, and she doesn't stop asking.

In the chapters that follow she keeps pressing how it could ever be made well, with so much harm in the world. Later she is told, in paraphrase, that she'll see it herself: that all manner of thing shall be well.
So the line doesn't end the question. It's a promise that keeps her company while the question stays open.
Some Christians who read Julian hold it that way; some readers take it simply as a line from a woman who asked honestly, and was answered gently.

how: Christians of several churches read Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love, and her line all shall be well is sometimes said or sung in prayer services and at times of grief.

o: a medieval mystic who asked why and heard a tender promise
an early English saint who copied the Gospels by hand
a medieval nun who explained exactly why God allows sin

games.q: inside Julian's answer — tap the pairs.
p: why wasn't sin stopped at the start?
fitting, something that had its place
tender, with no blame laid on her

s: Julian heard all shall be well on an easy, cheerful day
she writes that she was so ill the people around her thought she was dying.
the words answered her question about why sin wasn't stopped
she wondered why God didn't prevent it at the beginning; this was the reply.
the line says all is well right now
it's future tense: all shall be well. Julian keeps asking how in the chapters after.

games.q: you're Julian, very ill, asking why sin wasn't stopped at the beginning. an answer comes. what is it?
o: a promise, said tenderly: all shall be well.
games.why: she gets no reason and no blame; she gets a promise, and goes on asking how it can be true.

practice: Let one thing that isn't well right now come to mind, yours or someone else's. Then, once, silently and slowly, say Julian's line, sin was behovely, without repeating it to drown the hard thing out, and notice how it lands.
If it rings true, let it; if it rings false today, let that be honest too; if you pray, offer it as a promise; if not, hold it as a line from a book.

wordCard.voice: Julian, the medieval mystic who asked God why sin wasn't stopped at the start, and was answered not with a reason but a promise. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sin was behovely. A promise, while the question stays open. See you tomorrow.
